definition: A castle or large manor house. In France the word is also used for grand historic country houses and for wine estates.
Half-timbering: a visible wooden frame with the gaps filled in with plaster, brick or earth. Typical of Normandy and some other regions.
A long, low traditional farmhouse found mainly in Brittany and western France, with living space and outbuildings under one continuous roof.
Self-catering holiday accommodation, often a converted farm building or a small house.
An outbuilding that belongs to the main house, such as a barn, workshop or garage.
A label given to small French towns and villages that protect and promote a historic heritage.
A protected rural area where landscape, nature and local heritage are looked after while people live and work there.
A rural area of Normandy known for half-timbered houses, orchards, cider and cheese.
A historic area of the Pyrenees in the Ariège, around Saint-Girons.
A hilly wine-growing area of Languedoc in southern France.
In south-west France, a planned medieval market town built around a central square. In Provence, a country manor house.
A large, well-built house for a landowner or professional, with a more formal look than a farmhouse.
A traditional stone farmhouse of Provence and Languedoc.
A manor house, smaller than a château.
A dovecote: a small tower or building made to house pigeons.
A traditional cottage with a thatched roof.
A soft, pale limestone used to build many houses and châteaux in the Loire Valley.
A flat stone slab used instead of tiles for roofs in some mountain and hill regions.
Cut stone: blocks of dressed stone, used for fine walls and for door and window frames.
The energy performance rating shown on French property listings, from A (efficient) to G (poor).
A septic tank: private sewage treatment for homes that are not connected to the mains sewer.
A connection to the public mains sewer.
